title: Structural and physical properties of gyromorphs and disordered stealthy hyperuniform media
authors: Murray Skolnick, Riccardo Franchi, Luca Dal Negro, Paul J. Steinhardt, Salvatore Torquato
abstract: Disordered stealthy hyperuniform materials combine liquid-like statistical isotropy with crystal-like homogeneity, suppressed density fluctuations at large length scales, bounded holes, and an isotropic structure factor that vanishes for a finite range of wavevectors. This combination yields unusual physical properties, including optical transparency, effective delocalization, ultrafast spreadability, optimal conductivity, and complete isotropic photonic bandgaps. Gyromorphs, point patterns whose structure factor includes rings of Bragg-like peaks arranged with discrete $G$-fold rotational symmetry, were recently introduced as counterexamples: disordered media that can somehow achieve the same physical properties, in some cases with higher performance, without stealthiness or hyperuniformity. In this paper, we resolve the puzzle of how gyromorphs fit consistently with the stealthy hyperuniform studies. We first show that gyromorphs are actually hyperuniform and, in the large-$G$ limit where they become nearly isotropic, belong to the weakest form of hyperuniformity, known as Class III. Thus, gyromorphs should have comparatively degraded physical properties compared to stealthy hyperuniform media, which belong to the strongest form of hyperuniformity, known as Class I. We verify this expectation using the rigorous spectral Green's matrix method for the calculation of the density of states (DOS) and Purcell factors in large arrays of electric dipoles. We find that gyromorphs display size-dependent pseudogaps richly populated by localized states rather than smooth band gaps like those found for highly stealthy hyperuniform materials or in deterministic structures such as Vogel spiral and triangular lattices. Furthermore, we predict similar disorder-induced degradation relative to stealthy hyperuniformity with regard to transparency, spreadability and diffusion properties.
summary: The paper rigorously compares the structural and optical properties of gyromorphs against ideal stealthy hyperuniform materials. It concludes that while gyromorphs possess specific symmetries, their underlying structure places them in a lower hyperuniformity class (Class III). Consequently, they exhibit inferior physical performance compared to stealthy media, showing only localized pseudogaps instead of true photonic band gaps.
main_problem: The paper resolves the structural consistency of 'gyromorphs'—disordered point patterns with specific Bragg-like peaks—within the established hierarchy of disordered media compared to 'stealthy hyperuniform media.' It aims to compare their resulting physical properties, especially optical band gaps.
main_result: Gyromorphs are shown to belong to Class III hyperuniformity (the weakest form), predicting degraded physical properties relative to Class I stealthy hyperuniform media. Optically, gyromorphs exhibit only shallow pseudogaps filled with localized states, unlike the robust band gaps found in stealthy systems.
method: The analysis employs rigorous spectral Green's matrix methods for finite, nonperiodic arrays and full-wave density-of-states calculations using the MIT Photonic Bands code. Structural classification relies on analyzing scaling exponents of the local number variance ($\sigma^2_N(R)$).
model_or_system: The study compares three types of 2D disordered media: (1) Disordered Stealthy Hyperuniform Media (Class I), characterized by statistical isotropy and suppressed density fluctuations; (2) Gyromorphs, defined by Bragg-like peaks with discrete G-fold symmetry; and (3) benchmark structures like triangular lattices. The analysis is performed on finite arrays of resonant electric dipoles.
key_observables: Hyperuniformity exponent ($\alpha$), Density of States (DOS), Purcell factors, spectral gaps vs. pseudogaps, and time-dependent spreadability decay rates ($S(t)$).
important_parameters: The hyperuniformity class (I, II, III); the rotational symmetry order $G$; and the packing fraction ($\phi_2$) of the scatterers.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that structural classification via $\alpha$ dictates physical performance; it also notes that the Green's matrix method is necessary to handle nonperiodic media accurately.
figures_summary: Figures compare DOS maps and line cuts for various geometries (Triangular, SHU, Gyromorph), showing robust gaps in ordered/SHU systems versus pseudogaps filled with localized states in gyromorphs. Structural analysis plots confirm Class I vs. Class III scaling.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the structural definitions and theoretical framework of hyperuniformity classes. It then applies spectral Green's matrix methods to calculate optical properties (DOS, Purcell factors) for both stealthy and gyromorph structures. The core argument resolves the physical implications of the differing structural classes.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous link between abstract mathematical concepts in disordered media (hyperuniformity class $\alpha$) and measurable physical phenomena like photonic band gaps and light localization, which is highly relevant to designing metamaterials for quantum applications.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Representative images of (a) a stealthy hyperuniform point pattern with χ ≈0.49 and (b) a G = 60 gyromorph with Fourier ring radius KL/(2π). The structures in (a) and (b) each contain N = 1000 points and were prepared by taking circular cutouts of larger systems with N ∼104. As discussed below, the sample sizes used to ascertain their optical prop- erties are an order of magnitude larger.

FIG. 2. Log-log plots of the local number variance σ2 N(R) for χ = 0.49 stealthy and 24 ≤G ≤200 gyromorphs with Fourier ring radius KL/(2π) = 300. The inset highlights the large-R Class III hyperuniform scaling of the gyromorphs observed for 5 ≤Rρ1/2 ≤50. Note that only σ2 N(R) of higher G gyromorphs, which are effectively isotropic, are plotted here in order to keep them on equal footing with the truly isotropic stealthy hyperuniform systems.

FIG. 4. Area-normalized full-wave TM density of states D(ω) at the Γ point for periodic arrays of identical high-dielectric disks in air generated from stealthy hyperuniform systems with χ ≃0.49 and Class III random organization disk pat- terns with scaling exponent α = 0.42. The dielectric contrast is ϵ2/ϵ1 = 9 and the disk packing fraction is ϕ2 = 0.05. The stealthy hyperuniform system exhibits a TM band gap, with D(ω) = 0 over the indicated frequency interval at the reso- lution considered, whereas the random organization system exhibits only a shallow pseudogap with finite D(ω).

FIG. 3. Semilog plots of the void nearest-neighbor probability density HV (r) for stealthy hyperuniform systems with χ = 0.49, 24 ≤G ≤200 gyromorphs with Fourier ring radius KL/(2π) = 300. The plotted quantity is ρ−1/2HV (r). The dashed black lines highlight the exponential-like large-R tails of the G = 24, 60, 120 gyromorphs. Note that only HV (r) of higher G gyromorphs, which are effectively isotropic, are plotted here in order to keep them on equal footing with the truly isotropic stealthy hyperuniform systems.

FIG. 5. TM DOS maps for: (a) stealthy hyperuniform, and (b) gyromorph. The maps are plotted as a function of the normalized wavenumber k0ρ−1/2 and the normalized angular frequency (ω −ω0)/Γ0. Panels (a1)–(a3) and (b1)–(b3) display corresponding line cuts extracted from the DOS maps at k0ρ−1/2 = 1.60 (red dotted line), 2.50 (magenta dashed-dotted line), and 2.75 (black dotted line). Calculations are performed for arrays of N = 6500 dipoles, with a normalized angular frequency resolution of 8 × 10−3 in the DOS maps and 10−7 in the line cuts.
